To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we developed a combined AFM and lateral stretch device to perform indentation measurements on cells under mechanical strain and (2) that we found significant stiffenings of keratinocyte cell monolayers upon mechanical stretching, while a mutant keratin-deficient cell line showed a softening.

(i) repeated indentation at the same location in a single cell results in a stiffening at 50% strain, (ii) the stiffening is more pronounced in keratin-expressing cells, (iii) the stiffness of keratin-expressining cells is higher compared to keratin-devoid cells, and (iv) the difference is more pronounced at higher strains.

(1) the system allows for repeated indentation experiments on living cells under strain and (2) the system is suitable for the investigation of the role of intermediate filaments on cellular mechanics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanical behavior of living cells under high strain amplitudes and demonstrates the potential of our new system to investigate the mechanical properties of living cells.
a novel combined experimental system, which is suitable for the mechanical characterization of living cells at high strain amplitudes.
the development of an experimental setup to study the material properties of living cells at large strains.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the keratin cytoskeleton is responsible for the observed stiffening at high strains.
keratins stiffen cells at low strain amplitudes and soften them at high strain amplitudes, but that the overall effect depends on strain amplitude and keratin type.
the intermediate filaments in the cells are responsible for the stiffening.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
intermediate filaments are essential for cell stiffness and that they stiffen the cells at high strain amplitudes.
the system presented here is suitable for the investigation of the material properties of living cells at high strain amplitudes.

the AFM combined with a lateral stretch device enables microindentation analyses of living cells at high strains, which is a prerequisite for studying material properties of living cells in a physiological context.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of a lateral stretch device and an AFM allows the investigation of the mechanical properties of cells under physiological strain conditions.
the new experimental system is suitable for investigating the mechanical properties of living cells under high strains.
the combined AFM-lateral stretch system is a powerful tool for studying mechanical responses of living cells at high strains.
